title: Houthi Ballistic Missiles Strike Riyadh for First Time as Saudi Front Opens a New Phase; Iran Detains Tanker in Hormuz, Sets Seven Conditions for Talks
subhead: Yemen's Houthis fired ballistic missiles at Saudi Arabia's capital and struck oil infrastructure at Yanbu for the first time since the renewed war, bringing the conflict to the kingdom's doorstep as Iran issued a hard-line negotiating list via Qatar and detained an oil tanker in the Strait of Hormuz.

sections.heading: Houthi Missiles Reach Riyadh for the First Time
sections.body: The Houthi militia attacked Saudi Arabia's capital with a barrage of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones on Saturday, the first targeting of Riyadh since the renewed war, according to reporting from The New York Times via the Irish Times. Saudi Arabia confirmed a ballistic missile aimed at the capital was intercepted, after residents reported explosions and a plume of smoke near King Khalid International Airport, where FlightRadar24 showed major delays. The Saudi-led coalition said the Houthis also tried to strike civilian infrastructure in the Red Sea port city of Yanbu — where a key Saudi pipeline terminates — as well as Taif, Baysh and Farasan. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group fired a 'large number' of projectiles at 'sensitive sites' in Riyadh and at Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu, calling it retaliation for more than 700 Saudi airstrikes in Yemen.
sections.whyItMatters: Striking the capital — not just southern cities — is a step-change in the Houthi campaign and lands weeks before the Future Investment Initiative gathering in Riyadh. Chatham House analyst Farea Al-Muslimi called it a 'huge' escalation, reflecting Houthi confidence after recent battlefield gains; the group's ability to reach Yanbu means Saudi export infrastructure is now being targeted directly.

sections.heading: Iran Sets Seven Conditions for Talks Via Qatar, Warns of 'Decisive War'
sections.body: Iran has transmitted a seven-point list of conditions to Washington through Qatari mediators to start negotiations on ending the war, with security chief Mohsen Rezaei publicly warning that Tehran is prepared for a 'decisive war' if the demands are rejected, per Al Jazeera reporting cited by the New Indian Express. Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, told Al Jazeera the conditions include 'an end to the war on all fronts, the release of our frozen funds and an end to the naval blockade.' He said Qatar and Pakistan have been working to re-establish talks since a memorandum of understanding lapsed last month. Rezaei did not rule out another US strike, saying it was 'very much on the cards,' and confirmed Iran recently test-fired a multi-warhead anti-ship missile near a US vessel.
sections.whyItMatters: The list is a maximalist opening position — ending the US naval blockade and releasing frozen assets are preconditions the White House has resisted. But the fact Iran is transmitting demands through Qatar at all, ahead of UN General Assembly High-Level Week where the US State Department issued visas to Iran's delegation, keeps a diplomatic track alive even as the Houthi strikes suggest no de-escalation on the ground.

sections.heading: Revolutionary Guards Detain Tanker 'Trend' in the Strait of Hormuz
sections.body: Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they struck and detained the Togo-flagged oil tanker Trend in the Strait of Hormuz on Friday over what they called an 'illegal' attempted passage without permission, Marine Insight reported. The Guards' navy warned that ships trying to pass through the strait without authorisation face 'destruction.' Separately, the UK Maritime Trade Operations said a ship was hit by an 'unknown projectile' while sailing out of the strait early Friday, causing a fire that was extinguished with the crew reported safe; it was unclear whether this was the same vessel. The detention came as hundreds of thousands gathered in Tehran in the largest pro-government rally since the war began in late February.
sections.whyItMatters: The tanker detention shows that despite earlier signs of more than 80 percent of traffic diverting to an Omani route, Iran is still enforcing its control of the main waterway through selective interdiction — a tactic that keeps freight rates elevated (industry reports put tanker earnings past $1 million a day) without a full closure.

sections.heading: Trump Signs Russia-Iran Sanctions Law Targeting Shadow Fleet and Oil Buyers
sections.body: President Donald Trump signed the sweeping Russia-Iran sanctions bill into law on Friday, according to Reuters and Gulf News. The Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, named for the Republican senator, targets Moscow's revenues and Iran's economy, with provisions to hit the shadow oil fleet and, per National Herald India, allowing tariffs of up to 100 percent on countries buying Russian and Iranian oil and gas, including India and China. Reuters notes the White House statement confirmed the signing, which came amid opposition from Democrats who favored tougher Russia measures but opposed parts of the legislation.
sections.whyItMatters: The law formalises the sanctions architecture around the shadow fleet that moves sanctioned crude — directly relevant to India and China, the largest buyers of discounted Russian oil, and deepens the economic war against Iran on top of the naval blockade. How aggressively Trump enforces the tariff levers, given he retains broad discretion, will determine whether this is a bargaining chip or a real supply shock.

sections.heading: China and Russia Veto Extension of UN Iran Sanctions Panel
sections.body: China and Russia vetoed the extension of the UN panel monitoring sanctions against Iran under Security Council Resolution 2231, the mechanism that endorsed the 2015 nuclear deal, China Daily reported. The committee and its expert panel had been suspended under the resolution, and Britain, France and Germany last year triggered a snapback of measures following Iran's nuclear advances.
sections.whyItMatters: The veto deprives the Security Council of independent verification on Iran's compliance at the precise moment negotiations over a successor arrangement are being discussed. It strengthens Tehran's hand in any talks and signals Moscow and Beijing's continued willingness to shield Iran from multilateral pressure.

sections.heading: Europe Enters Winter With Record-Low Gas Storage and Hormuz Still Closed
sections.body: European gas storage is only about 70 percent full — a record low for this point in the year — as the continent heads into winter with the Strait of Hormuz still effectively shut, according to Reuters and a Reuters Breakingviews analysis. Global LNG prices could spike further as North Asian buyers compete with Europe for cargoes, with spot LNG prices reportedly up around 150 percent. Bloomberg, via Yahoo Finance, reports European winter power prices are at their highest since the 2022 energy crisis. One mitigating factor, per Breakingviews, is a warmer El Niño winter and the return of some Qatari supply via rerouted cargoes. Separately, an opinion piece on IJR notes Cheniere Energy completed Stage 3 of its Corpus Christi LNG facility on August 28, adding new US export capacity that is capturing demand Qatar cannot fill while Hormuz is shut.
sections.whyItMatters: A 70 percent fill rate versus the usual 90-plus percent target leaves Europe exposed to a cold snap, and the closure of Hormuz has cut off the region's main flexible supplier Qatar at the worst possible moment. US LNG is the main beneficiary of Qatar's loss, a lasting shift in the Atlantic basin supply map.

sections.heading: Pakistan Pressures Iran Over Energy Supplies as Import Bills Bite
sections.body: Pakistan's Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar urged Iran to ensure uninterrupted energy supplies and safe shipping in a call with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, Pakistan Today and Arab News reported, as the Middle East war disrupts regional trade. The appeal comes as Pakistan implements austerity measures including a 50 percent cut in fuel allocations for official vehicles amid an energy crunch, per Outlook India.
sections.whyItMatters: A rare, direct Pakistani request to Tehran over energy shows the war's economic fallout is spreading to South Asia, where Pakistan depends on affordable energy imports and cannot absorb tanker-rate spikes or supply interruptions. It also signals Islamabad is pressing for moderation even as Qatari mediation on Iran-US talks continues.

bottomLine: The Iran war's Saudi front escalated sharply when Houthi ballistic missiles struck Riyadh for the first time and reached the Yanbu oil terminal, while Iran simultaneously hardened its negotiating position — seven preconditions via Qatar backed by a 'decisive war' warning — and detained a tanker in Hormuz. The juxtaposition is the key signal: Tehran is keeping a diplomatic track alive through the UNGA window while its proxies escalate militarily, and sanctions pressure tightened with Trump signing the Russia-Iran law and Moscow and Beijing vetoing UN monitoring. With European gas storage at a record low and Hormuz still closed, the energy system heads into winter carrying elevated prices and tanker rates, with US LNG the main structural beneficiary of Qatar's forced absence.
sources: Irish Times/New York Times, NBC News, Marine Insight/CNA/AP, Al Jazeera via New Indian Express, Ynetnews, Reuters, Gulf News, National Herald India, China Daily, Bloomberg via Yahoo Finance, Reuters Breakingviews, OilPrice.com, IJR, Pakistan Today, Arab News, Outlook India
